extraction.research_question: Can single-source shortest paths (SSSP) on directed graphs with real non-negative edge weights be solved faster than Dijkstra's O(m + n log n) bound on sparse graphs, in the comparison-addition model, and can the Omega(n log n) sorting barrier be broken for this problem?
extraction.theory: Dijkstra's algorithm sorts vertices by distance through a priority queue, which costs Theta(n log n) on the frontier. Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges in k rounds with no sorting. The paper merges the two ideas through recursive partitioning, in the style of bottleneck-path algorithms (Gabow-Tarjan 1988; Chechik et al. 2016; Duan et al. 2018), so that the frontier is shrunk to pivots before any sorting (pp. 2-4). The sorting cost is reduced by a block-based partial-sorting structure (Lemma 3.3, pp. 6-7). The paper does not present a behavioural or social theory.
extraction.data: No empirical data. The analysis is over worst-case inputs: directed graph G=(V,E) with n vertices, m edges, and non-negative real weights w: E to R>=0. The algorithm first transforms G into a constant-degree graph G' with O(m) vertices and O(m) edges via zero-weight cycles (Sec. 2, p. 3). The bound assumes m = O(n) (p. 4). No sample, N, or time period applies.
extraction.method: Deterministic algorithm design plus worst-case running-time analysis. The core procedure is a recursive bounded multi-source shortest path routine, BMSSP(l, B, S) (Algorithm 3, p. 10). It uses FindPivots (Algorithm 1, p. 6), a base case that is a mini-Dijkstra (Algorithm 2, p. 9), and a partial-sort block-list data structure D (Lemma 3.3, pp. 6-8). Parameters are k = floor(log^(1/3) n) and t = floor(log^(2/3) n), with recursion depth ceil(log n / t) (Sec. 3.1, p. 4). Correctness is proved by induction on level l (Lemma 3.7, pp. 12-13). Time is bounded in Lemma 3.12 (p. 14).
extraction.identification: Not applicable. This is a worst-case complexity result, not a statistical or causal identification strategy.
extraction.scope: Population: directed graphs with real non-negative weights, sparse regime m = O(n) after a constant-degree transformation. Model: comparison-addition only (each addition and comparison takes unit time; no other operations on weights). Era: 2025 arXiv preprint. Institutions: Tsinghua University, Stanford University, and Max Planck Institute for Informatics (author affiliations, p. 2 footnotes). The paper does not address lobbying, networks as social objects, elections, persuasion, turnout, legislators, or text measurement.

key_findings.finding: Main result: a deterministic SSSP algorithm for directed graphs with real non-negative weights in time O(m log^(2/3) n), the first to break the O(m + n log n) bound of Dijkstra on sparse graphs.
key_findings.numbers: O(m log^(2/3) n)

key_findings.finding: The result is also the first deterministic algorithm to beat O(m + n log n) for SSSP even on undirected graphs, since the prior O(m sqrt(log n log log n)) SSSP algorithm of Duan, Mao, Shu, Yin (DMSY23) is randomized.
key_findings.location: Sec. 1, p. 2 (remark after Theorem 1.1); DMSY23 cited on p. 1
key_findings.numbers: DMSY23: O(m sqrt(log n log log n)) randomized, undirected

key_findings.finding: Dijkstra is optimal if the output must include the vertex ordering by distance (Haeupler et al. 2024), so the improvement applies to distances without a full ordering.
key_findings.location: Sec. 1, p. 1 (citing HHR+24); Sec. 3.1 p. 4 ('without necessarily recovering a complete ordering')

key_findings.finding: Key idea: shrink the frontier. For a bound B, the frontier S is reduced to pivots of size at most |eU|/k, where k = log^(Omega(1)) n. Each pivot roots a shortest-path tree of at least k vertices.
key_findings.location: Technical overview, Sec. 1.1, p. 2; FindPivots Lemma 3.2, p. 5
key_findings.numbers: |W| = O(k|S|); |P| <= |W|/k <= |eU|/k; time O(min{k^2|S|, k|eU|})

key_findings.finding: Per-vertex running time is reduced from Theta(log n) to log n / log^(Omega(1)) n through divide-and-conquer over log n / t levels.
key_findings.numbers: log n / log^(Omega(1))(n) per vertex

key_findings.finding: Parameter choice that yields the final bound: k = floor(log^(1/3) n), t = floor(log^(2/3) n), recursion level l = ceil(log n / t).
key_findings.location: Sec. 3.1, p. 4; Lemma 3.12 final statement, p. 14
key_findings.numbers: k = floor(log^(1/3) n); t = floor(log^(2/3) n); l = ceil(log n / t)

key_findings.finding: Output-size bound for each BMSSP call: the returned set U has size at most 4k^(2lt), and a partial run has |U| at least k^(2lt).
key_findings.numbers: |U| <= 4k^(2lt); partial case |U| >= k^(2lt)

key_findings.finding: Running-time bound for a BMSSP call at level l.
key_findings.numbers: C(k + 2t/k)(l+1)|U| + C(t + l log k)|N+_[min S d(x), B)(U)|

key_findings.finding: Total running time over recursion depth: depth is O(log^(1/3) n) and FindPivots costs O(nk) per depth, so the sum is O(nk (log n)/t) = O(n log^(2/3) n). Batch-prepend overhead is O(n log^(1/3) n log log n).
key_findings.numbers: depth O(log^(1/3) n); per-depth cost O(nk); overall O(n log^(2/3) n); batch-prepend O(n log^(1/3) n log log n)

key_findings.finding: Structure of recursion: children's output sets U_y are disjoint, and the sum of |U_x| over all nodes of the recursion tree is O(n log n / t).
key_findings.numbers: sum |U_x| = O(n (log n)/t)

key_findings.finding: Data structure D (partial sorting with block lists) supports insert in amortized O(max{1, log(N/M)}), batch prepend in O(L max{1, log(L/M)}), and pull in O(|S'|).
key_findings.numbers: insert O(max{1, log(N/M)}); batch prepend O(L max{1, log(L/M)}); pull O(|S'|)

key_findings.finding: Correctness: BMSSP returns the full set of vertices whose shortest path visits S, with all returned vertices complete. The top-level call with S = {s}, B = infinity finds all shortest paths.

limitations: Theoretical only. The text reports no implementation or experiments, so practical constants are unmeasured. The hidden constant C in the bounds is not quantified.

Computation model is the comparison-addition model only (real weights; each addition and comparison costs unit time). Integer-weight or word-RAM improvements are discussed as related work (Thorup 1999/2004), not as this paper's result.

Assumes constant in- and out-degree via a transformation (Sec. 2, p. 3). The transformation is stated to preserve shortest paths and yield O(m) vertices and edges. Assumes m >= n-1 and every vertex reachable from s (p. 3-4).
Assumes all path lengths are distinct (Assumption 2.1, p. 4). The paper argues a lexicographic tuple order makes this WLOG, using Pred[] and hop count alpha stored per bd[v] (p. 4).

Bound is O(m log^(2/3) n), which is superlinear on sparse graphs; the paper does not claim linear time. The result is for distances and does not produce the full distance ordering. The paper cites HHR+24 that Dijkstra is optimal if ordering is required (p. 1).
Partial executions of BMSSP are noted as more complex to analyze, and the paper introduces batch-prepend and FindPivots to handle them (Sec. 3.1, p. 5; Lemma 3.3, p. 7).

summary_md:
Duan, Mao, Mao, Shu and Yin (arXiv 2504.17033v2, 2025; Paul's bib lists it as STOC 2025) give a deterministic single-source shortest-path algorithm for **directed** graphs with real non-negative weights that runs in O(m log^(2/3) n) in the comparison-addition model. It is the first to beat Dijkstra's O(m + n log n) on sparse graphs. The method combines Dijkstra with Bellman-Ford through a recursive bounded multi-source routine (BMSSP). FindPivots shrinks the frontier to at most |U|/k pivots, and a block-list structure sorts only partially, with k = log^(1/3) n and t = log^(2/3) n. The result covers distances only, with no full distance ordering. It is purely theoretical: there is no implementation, and the constant C is never given.

For Paul's systems this is a speed result with very little to transfer. Every route engine as built is either tiny (533 members, an O(N^2) array scan in the dashboard), a point-to-sink query that stops early (staffer closeness routes, bidirectional, plus Yen alternatives), or an integer-weight search (overlap routes). The paper's bound covers full single-source distances on sparse graphs with real weights, so none of these uses fits its model. The one real link is Assumption 2.1: the paper breaks ties by lexicographic order on (length, hop count, predecessor), which matches the staffer router's (cost, steps) tie rule. On latency, the staffer-network lane found the bottleneck was memory (pair_cache), not the heap's log n. ALT landmarks remain the deferred lever, and this paper does not replace them. While checking the dashboard's 'provably optimal' chain, I found a possible problem with edge direction (see flags). It is UNVERIFIED.

extraction.document_type: Journal article (open access, CC BY). Titled a systematic review, but the body is a single-environment benchmark of four pathfinding algorithms plus a descriptive literature comparison. No review protocol (databases, search strings, inclusion rules, paper counts) is reported.
extraction.coverage: Full text read: the entire extracted text file (1,811 lines, journal pages 1-30 including references 1-95), in chunks of about 400 lines. Annotation file read in full: 68 entries (67 highlights, 1 free-text note). Metadata hint confirmed against the PDF header; authors' full names added. No parts skipped.
extraction.identification: None. Descriptive benchmark: the same grids are fed to each algorithm and the outputs are ranked. There is no causal design, no controls for hardware or run-to-run variance, and no repeated trials. Theory section is a taxonomy (uninformed / informed-heuristic / metaheuristic), not a tested hypothesis.
extraction.theory: Taxonomy only. Pathfinding is split into uninformed (BFS, Dijkstra), informed/heuristic (A*, Greedy Best First, D* Lite, HPA*, JPS) and metaheuristic (GA, ACO) families, and static vs dynamic. The paper argues heuristic methods save time by pruning the search space (Sections 2, 3.2). No formal model is stated beyond the cost functions F(n)=G(n)+H(n) and the Table 2 complexity expressions.
extraction.research_question: Which of four pathfinding algorithms (Dijkstra, A*, Breadth First Search, Greedy Best First) performs best on 2D square grids of size 4x4 to 32x32, with and without obstacles, in terms of execution time, total iteration blocks, computed blocks and shortest path length, so that game developers can choose one? Secondary: how do the families compare in the literature on memory and time (Table 5).
extraction.data: Synthetic game-style grids generated in the Unity engine: 2D square (octile) grids of 4x4, 8x8, 16x16 and 32x32 cells, each run with and without obstacles. Unit = one algorithm run on one grid configuration. Reported cells: 4 algorithms x 4 sizes x 2 conditions = 32 algorithm-by-grid results (16 rows in each of Tables 3 and 4). Not reported: number of repetitions, start and goal placement, obstacle layout or density, the iteration count k, hardware, and run dates. Literature input for Section 3 and Table 5: 95 references, span 1959 to 2022 (count of papers actually screened not stated). No real-world dataset.
extraction.method: Implemented BFS, Dijkstra, A* and Greedy Best First in Unity (Algorithms 1-4; the "GRIN_PF" Algorithm 6 is a harness that loops over these four). Per run recorded: total iteration blocks, total computed blocks excluding the shortest path, execution time in ms, and shortest path length in blocks (Section 5, p.19-20). Results compared as within-size rankings and narrative (Section 6, p.23-26). Theoretical side: asymptotic time/space table (Table 2, p.14) and a pairwise literature comparison table with category, time, memory, implemented yes/no, and cited source (Table 5, p.26-27). No statistical tests, confidence intervals, or repeated timings. Memory was not measured.
extraction.scope: Population: single-agent pathfinding on regular 2D square grids in a game-style environment. Dynamic obstacles and 3D, hexagonal, triangular or irregular (waypoint, visibility graph, navmesh) grids are discussed but not tested. summary_md:
Lawande et al. (2022) call the paper a systematic review, but it is really a benchmark of four algorithms on one setup: BFS, Dijkstra, A* and Greedy Best First (GBF), each run once on Unity square grids from 4x4 to 32x32, with and without obstacles. It reports no search protocol, no repeated trials, no hardware details and no measured memory, so its memory rankings and the Table 5 citations (several of which do not match the claims) cannot be relied on. The usable results are narrow. With no obstacles, GBF is fastest at every size; Dijkstra is 2.8x to 21.6x slower than GBF, and all four find the same path length. With obstacles, GBF stays fastest from 8x8 up, but its paths get longer (37 vs 31 at 16x16, 81 vs 75 at 32x32). A* expands fewer nodes than Dijkstra on the larger grids (587 vs 754 iterations at 32x32) and still returns the optimal length. D* and D* Lite are only described, never tested. The proposed GRIN_PF is just a loop that runs the four existing algorithms.

What this means for the system as built is mostly a check on design choices, not new evidence. The one sharp bearing comes from the paper's GBF-with-obstacles result. The dashboard's recruitment path first runs an exact max-product Dijkstra backward from the target (`distToTarget`), then walks forward greedily, choosing at each hop the neighbour with the highest edge probability times its precomputed reliability to the target. That walk is optimal only while the precomputed reliabilities are exact. Once a user drops members, the walk skips them but the reliabilities are still computed through them. The walk then becomes a greedy best-first search on an out-of-date estimate, which is the case where the paper shows longer, non-optimal paths. Terrier's walk router already does textbook A* with an admissible straight-line estimate, which is the setting where the paper's A* result applies best. For the non-spatial social graphs, the paper offers no usable heuristic.

summary_md: Kumar, Mallik, Khetarpal and Panda (Information Sciences 607, 2022) propose SGNN, which treats influence maximization as a pseudo-regression task. Each node gets a struc2vec structural-identity embedding. A GNN regressor with LSTM neighbourhood aggregation is trained on labels made by simulating every node's individual spread under SIR and IC diffusion. The training network is chosen by a parametric sweep over synthetic graphs. The trained model then predicts node influence on an unseen target network, and the top-k predicted nodes become the seed set. The authors report that SGNN beats classical and recent IM baselines on several real networks under SIR and IC. The local text is only a ScienceDirect preview, so datasets, network sizes, metrics, effect sizes and limitations cannot be checked. Every performance claim here is the authors' own and is UNVERIFIED. The paper's stated motivation is cost: greedy IM is accurate and has a guarantee but is expensive, while centrality heuristics are cheap but network-specific. For Melange the cost argument mostly does not apply. The budget frontier already runs lazy (CELF-style) greedy with common random numbers on a single 533-member chamber graph and caps at 60 seeds, so the expensive side of the trade-off is affordable. Three features of SGNN also clash with choices Melange made on purpose. Seeds are ranked by each node's standalone spread, which ignores overlap between seeds. The embedding has no stance or direction, the same reason InfluenceScore was retired. And the labels come from single-colour diffusion, not the competitive two-colour race the engine models. The paper is best read as a scale-motivated alternative that Melange does not need, and as a caution against top-k standalone ranking.

extraction.research_question: How can the most reliable path, the path that maximizes the probability of arriving on time for a fixed travel-time budget, be found exactly and efficiently in large road networks with stochastic link travel times? (Abstract; Sec. 1, pp. 3-5.)
extraction.theory: Travel-time reliability is defined as the on-time arrival probability, P(T <= b), with path travel times treated as normal, so maximizing reliability is equivalent to minimizing z = (b - mean)/SD. The objective is non-additive, so Dijkstra-type methods do not apply. Solution logic rests on first-order stochastic dominance (FSD, Prop. 1), Mean-Budget (M-B) dominance (Prop. 3, from Chen et al. 2013a), and monotonicity of the objective under path extension (Lemmas 1-3). Risk-taking regimes (risk-averse, neutral, seeking) are set by the z-value of the least expected time path (Prop. 2, p. 8). No behavioral theory is tested empirically.
extraction.data: Case study on the Wuhan, China road network: 19,306 nodes and 46,757 links. Link travel times come from floating-car GPS data from 11,248 taxis reporting about every 40 seconds, map-matched with the MDP-MM algorithm, which the authors say reaches over 90% accuracy in prior work. Data cover five weekdays, 14-18 September 2009, 7-10 a.m. (Sec. 4.1, pp. 14-15). Unit of analysis: link and path travel times, and origin-destination (O-D) pairs. Link fits use chi-square tests at 5% across normal, lognormal and gamma distributions. Monte Carlo validation uses 100 randomly selected paths. Computational tests use 100 random O-D pairs per network, averaged over 100 runs, on four additional networks from Chen et al. (2013a): Chicago regional (12,982 nodes, 39,018 links), G1 (2,000 nodes, 7,820 links), G2 (5,000 nodes, 19,700 links), and G3 (10,000 nodes, 39,600 links). The paper does not report a count of O-D pairs for the single numerical example.
extraction.method: Two-stage exact algorithm, MRP-TS. Stage 1: a deterministic A* or Dijkstra search finds the least expected time path, which gives an upper or lower bound on the optimal reliability and sets the risk regime (Prop. 2). Stage 2: a multi-criteria label-setting procedure, MRP-RS for risk-seeking (fixed confidence level, Sec. 3.1) and MRP-RA for risk-averse (adaptive confidence level starting at 0.999, z = 3.5, with an admissible heuristic h(i), Sec. 3.2). Risk-neutral cases return the least expected time path directly. Optimality is argued through Props. 4-5 and Lemmas 1-3. Complexity is analyzed in Sec. 3.3. Benchmarks: the authors' improved multi-criteria label-correcting BSP-LC (Nie and Wu 2009 extended with a bi-criteria method, Appendix B, valid only for normal times), and multi-criteria A* from Chen et al. (2013a) used to check that MRP-TS returns the same paths. Implemented in Visual C#, one core of a 2.0 GHz i7 laptop, Windows 7. Identification strategy: not applicable; this is an algorithmic and computational paper with no causal design.
extraction.scope: Population: road travelers in a congested city network, modeled as a directed graph with stochastic link times. Institution: none. Era: data from 2009 morning peaks; paper published 2016. Geography: one Chinese city plus four synthetic or benchmark networks. Restrictions: road transport only; link travel times independent; O-D pairs randomly sampled; reliability computed in model terms, not validated against observed arrivals.

limitations: Link travel-time correlations are omitted for simplicity; the paper proposes a two-level hierarchical model as a future extension (Sec. 5, p. 20).
Only road transport is modeled; multimodal networks are left to future work (p. 20).
The method is not extended to en-route traffic information updated during the trip (p. 20).
Normal approximation of path travel times is only approximate, with weaker accuracy at the 90th percentile due to skew (p. 16). It was validated on only 100 Monte Carlo paths.
Worst-case complexity is non-polynomial in theory (|P| grows exponentially); efficiency depends on the practical size of the non-dominated set in sparse networks (Sec. 3.3, p. 14).

The main benchmark, BSP-LC, is the authors' own improved variant (Appendix B, pp. 24-25), valid only for normal path times. Runtime comparisons come from one implementation on one laptop, reported in milliseconds.

The case study is one city, five weekday morning peaks in 2009, with floating-car data from taxis. Map-matching accuracy (over 90%) is taken from prior work. O-D pairs and budgets are randomly sampled or derived from alpha using A*.
Optimality of MRP-RA depends on an admissible heuristic; the Euclidean and least-expected-time heuristics are the examples given (pp. 12-13).
Reliability is an analytic probability under the model. The paper does not compare predicted on-time probabilities with observed arrivals.
Independence of link times is assumed, and the authors note the correlated-link case is handled only by reference to prior work (p. 5).

summary_md:
Chen, Shi, Zhang, Lam, Li and Xiang study a road-routing problem. Each link has a random travel time, and the goal is the path with the highest probability of arriving within a fixed time budget b, P(T <= b). They treat path times as normal, so this means minimizing (b - mean)/SD. Because path SD is the square root of summed variances, the objective is non-additive, and the authors state that Dijkstra-type methods cannot solve it. Their exact two-stage algorithm, MRP-TS, works as follows. A deterministic least-expected-time search first fixes the risk regime. Mean-Budget dominance with multi-criteria label-setting then finds the optimum. They check optimality by matching an independent multi-criteria A* on the same budgets. On Wuhan taxi data (19,306 nodes, 2009 morning peaks), the best path changes with b: a short budget picks a high-variance path and a long budget picks a low-variance one. MRP-TS runs in milliseconds, about 750x faster than the label-correcting benchmark on Chicago. Links are assumed independent, and the authors name correlation as the main open limitation.

What this means for Paul's system is narrow. The dashboard's recruitment chain (`make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:735-757`) cites this paper as grounding for its max-product path. That path is a different problem: the classical product-of-independent-probabilities path, which is additive in -log p and correctly solved by Dijkstra. This paper is about deadline-reliability, which is the case Dijkstra cannot handle. So the citation supports the word 'reliable', not the method. The paper's useful lessons are elsewhere. Exact optimality claims should be checked against a second algorithm, as Chen et al. do. Products of independent per-hop probabilities overstate certainty when the hops are correlated. And a true deadline or variance penalty on a recruitment chain would need label-setting, not Dijkstra. Nothing here concerns lobbying, legislators or elections.

bearings.paper_claim: The paper's 'most reliable path' maximizes on-time arrival probability Phi((b - mean)/SD) for a travel-time budget b. It states that this objective 'is non-additive and cannot be solved by existing' shortest-path methods, so it uses M-B dominance plus multi-criteria label-setting (MRP-TS) rather than Dijkstra.

bearings.system_side: The recruitment chain is a max-product path: distToTarget runs a Dijkstra-style max-product search and tracePath follows the argmax of PE*dT. Reliability is the product of per-hop kernel probabilities, and chainHold is the product of activeP(p) with ASKM 0.07. The code comment cites Chen, Shi, Zhang & Lam 2016 as grounding for 'maximize the probability the whole chain holds' and calls the result 'PROVABLY-OPTIMAL'. A product of independent edge probabilities is additive in -log p (the Frank / Bellman reliable-path case), so Dijkstra is the right tool. That object is not the one this paper solves.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports the system's method only in name. Its deadline-reliability algorithm would carry over only if the system modeled a stochastic time-to-join per hop and asked for P(target joins before a deadline such as markup), which it does not. As built, the right grounding is the classical max-product or -log p shortest path, not this paper. Road data, 2009 Wuhan; no legislative content.
